claim: President George H. W. Bush used the phrase "a new world order" in an address before a joint session of Congress on September 11, 1990. The speech was about the Persian Gulf crisis — Iraq's invasion of Kuwait five weeks earlier — and set out five objectives for the American response. The fifth was the phrase itself: "Out of these troubled times, our fifth objective — a new world order — can emerge: a new era — freer from the threat of terror, stronger in the pursuit of justice, and more secure in the quest for peace." The subject was the post-Cold War settlement and the coalition against Iraq, not terrorism policy; the reference to terror is one clause in a list.

sources.label: George H. W. Bush, "Address Before a Joint Session of the Congress on the Persian Gulf Crisis and the Federal Budget Deficit," September 11, 1990 — transcript.
sources.quote: Out of these troubled times, our fifth objective—a new world order—can emerge

sources.label: The Washington Post, "Bush: 'Out of These Troubled Times . . . A New World Order'," September 12, 1990 — next-day transcript of the address.
C-SPAN, video of the September 11, 1990 joint-session address.

notes: The date and the phrase are both real and are regularly cited as a September 11 pattern. What the speech was actually about is the part that gets dropped: Kuwait, oil, the coalition, and the federal budget deficit, which shares the address's official title. Miller Center hosts the Public Papers text.
